attributes.title: Terraform Remote State on AWS S3 with State Locking
attributes.summary: Move Terraform state off your laptop: create a versioned, encrypted S3 bucket, turn on native state locking, migrate existing state, set IAM permissions and fix stuck locks.
attributes.content:
The first time you run Terraform, it writes a file called `terraform.tfstate` next to your code. That's fine while you're learning. It stops being fine the moment a second person, or a CI pipeline, needs to run `terraform apply`. This guide moves state to an S3 bucket with locking, so a team can share it safely.

## Why local state breaks down

Terraform's state file is its memory: the mapping between the resources in your code and the real resources in AWS. Keeping it on one laptop causes three problems:

- **No sharing.** Your teammate's Terraform doesn't know what yours created, so it tries to create everything again.
- **No locking.** Two `apply` runs at the same time can corrupt the state or create duplicate resources.
- **Secrets on disk.** State often contains passwords, keys and connection strings in plain text.

A remote backend fixes all three: one shared copy, a lock while someone is running, and storage you can encrypt and control access to.

> **Key idea:** never commit `terraform.tfstate` to Git. Add `*.tfstate`, `*.tfstate.*` and `.terraform/` to your `.gitignore`.

## Step 1: Create the state bucket

The bucket has to exist before Terraform can use it, so create it once by hand (or in a small separate Terraform project). Pick a globally unique name:

```bash
BUCKET=mycompany-terraform-state
REGION=ap-south-1

aws s3api create-bucket \
  --bucket "$BUCKET" \
  --region "$REGION" \
  --create-bucket-configuration LocationConstraint="$REGION"

# Keep every old version of the state, so you can recover from a bad apply
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning \
  --bucket "$BUCKET" \
  --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled

# Encrypt state at rest
aws s3api put-bucket-encryption \
  --bucket "$BUCKET" \
  --server-side-encryption-configuration \
  '{"Rules":[{"ApplyServerSideEncryptionByDefault":{"SSEAlgorithm":"AES256"}}]}'

# Make sure the bucket can never be made public
aws s3api put-public-access-block \
  --bucket "$BUCKET" \
  --public-access-block-configuration \
  BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true
```

> **Note:** In `us-east-1`, leave out `--create-bucket-configuration`. It's the only region that rejects it.

**Versioning is the most important setting here.** If an apply goes wrong or someone deletes the state, you can restore the previous version from the S3 console in a minute.

## Step 2: Configure the backend

Add a `backend` block to your Terraform configuration, for example in `backend.tf`:

```hcl
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.10"

  backend "s3" {
    bucket       = "mycompany-terraform-state"
    key          = "prod/network/terraform.tfstate"
    region       = "ap-south-1"
    encrypt      = true
    use_lockfile = true
  }
}
```

- **`key`** is the path of the state file inside the bucket. Give each project and environment its own key.
- **`encrypt`** makes Terraform request server-side encryption when it writes the file.
- **`use_lockfile`** turns on locking with a small `.tflock` file stored next to the state in S3. It needs Terraform 1.10 or newer.

> **Older setups:** before Terraform 1.10, locking needed a DynamoDB table set with `dynamodb_table = "terraform-locks"`. That option is now deprecated. If you're on an older version, upgrade if you can; if not, the DynamoDB table still works.

## Step 3: Move your existing state

If you already have a local `terraform.tfstate`, Terraform can copy it to S3 for you:

```bash
terraform init -migrate-state
```

Terraform asks whether to copy the existing state to the new backend. Answer `yes`, then check that nothing changed:

```bash
terraform plan
# No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration.
```

If the plan is clean, the migration worked. You can now delete the local `terraform.tfstate` and its `.backup` file.

## Step 4: Give people and pipelines the right permissions

Anyone or anything that runs Terraform needs these S3 permissions on the state bucket, in addition to the permissions for the resources it manages:

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "s3:ListBucket",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::mycompany-terraform-state"
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::mycompany-terraform-state/prod/network/terraform.tfstate"
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject", "s3:DeleteObject"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::mycompany-terraform-state/prod/network/terraform.tfstate.tflock"
    }
  ]
}
```

Scoping access to specific keys lets you give a team access to their own state without letting them read anyone else's. For a looser setup, use `prod/*` instead of a single key.

## Step 5: One state per environment

Don't put dev, staging and production in one state file. A mistake in dev shouldn't be able to touch production. The simplest approach is a different `key` per environment.

To avoid copying the backend block, leave out the values that change and pass them at `init` time (this is called partial configuration):

```hcl
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket       = "mycompany-terraform-state"
    region       = "ap-south-1"
    encrypt      = true
    use_lockfile = true
  }
}
```

```bash
# Development
terraform init -backend-config="key=dev/network/terraform.tfstate"

# Production
terraform init -reconfigure -backend-config="key=prod/network/terraform.tfstate"
```

`-reconfigure` tells Terraform to switch backends without trying to copy state across. That's what you want when moving between environments.

## Step 6: When a lock gets stuck

If a run is cancelled halfway, for example a CI job times out, the lock can be left behind. The next run fails with:

```text
Error: Error acquiring the state lock
Lock Info:
  ID:        6f1c2a7e-3b0d-4a9e-9c55-2f1e7d8b4c10
  Path:      mycompany-terraform-state/prod/network/terraform.tfstate
  Operation: OperationTypeApply
  Who:       runner@github-actions
  Created:   2026-10-28 09:14:03 UTC
```

**First make sure nobody is really running Terraform.** Check the `Who` and `Created` fields, and look at your CI runs. If it's truly stale, release it with the lock ID:

```bash
terraform force-unlock 6f1c2a7e-3b0d-4a9e-9c55-2f1e7d8b4c10
```

Never force-unlock a lock that's still in use. Two applies at once is exactly what locking is there to prevent.

## Common problems

| Error | Likely cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `NoSuchBucket` on `init` | Bucket name or region is wrong | Check `bucket` and `region` in the backend block |
| `AccessDenied` on `init` or `plan` | Missing S3 permissions | Compare the IAM policy with Step 4, including the `.tflock` key |
| `Backend configuration changed` | You changed the backend block | Run `terraform init -migrate-state` (to move state) or `-reconfigure` (to switch) |
| `Unsupported argument "use_lockfile"` | Terraform is older than 1.10 | Upgrade Terraform, or use `dynamodb_table` instead |
| Plan wants to recreate everything | Wrong `key`, so Terraform sees an empty state | Point `key` at the right state file |

## Wrapping up

Remote state is one of the first things to set up on any real Terraform project. A versioned, encrypted S3 bucket plus `use_lockfile = true` gives your team one source of truth, protects you from overlapping applies, and lets you recover when something goes wrong. Once it's in place, running Terraform from a CI pipeline is the natural next step.

attributes.title: Deploy to Kubernetes with GitHub Actions
attributes.summary: A complete CI/CD pipeline: test the code, build a Docker image, push it to GitHub Container Registry and roll it out to Kubernetes, with safe rollouts and one-command rollbacks.
attributes.content:
A good pipeline turns "it works on my machine" into "it's running in the cluster" without anyone typing `kubectl` by hand. In this guide I'll build one with GitHub Actions that tests the code, builds a Docker image, pushes it to GitHub Container Registry (GHCR), and rolls it out to Kubernetes, with a safe way back if something goes wrong.

## What we're building

Every push to `main` runs three jobs, one after another:

1. **Test**: run the unit tests. If they fail, nothing else runs.
2. **Build**: build the Docker image and push it to `ghcr.io`, tagged with the commit SHA.
3. **Deploy**: point the Kubernetes Deployment at the new image and wait for the rollout to finish.

```text
push to main ──► test ──► build & push image ──► deploy to Kubernetes
                              ghcr.io/<owner>/<app>:<sha>
```

> **Key idea:** tag every image with the commit SHA, not just `latest`. Then every running pod points at an exact commit, and rolling back is just deploying an older tag.

## Prerequisites

- A repository with a `Dockerfile` that builds your app.
- A Kubernetes cluster you can reach from the internet (EKS, GKE, AKS, or any cluster with a public API endpoint).
- A Deployment already running in the cluster, for example one created with `kubectl apply -f k8s/`.

## Step 1: A small, production-ready Dockerfile

Use a multi-stage build so the final image only contains what the app needs at runtime. Here's an example for a Node.js app:

```dockerfile
# Build stage: install everything and build
FROM node:20-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

# Runtime stage: only production dependencies and the build output
FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
USER node
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"]
```

Two details matter here. Copying `package*.json` before the rest of the code lets Docker cache the `npm ci` layer, so builds are fast when only code changes. And `USER node` means the container doesn't run as root.

## Step 2: Give the pipeline access to the cluster

The deploy job needs a kubeconfig. Don't use your personal admin one. Create a ServiceAccount that can only update Deployments in one namespace:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: github-deployer
  namespace: my-app
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: deployer
  namespace: my-app
rules:
  - apiGroups: ["apps"]
    resources: ["deployments"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "patch"]
  - apiGroups: ["apps"]
    resources: ["replicasets"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: github-deployer
  namespace: my-app
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: github-deployer
    namespace: my-app
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: deployer
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
```

Then build a kubeconfig that uses this ServiceAccount's token, reusing the server address and CA certificate from your current context:

```bash
# A token for the ServiceAccount (valid for 1 year here; rotate it before it expires)
TOKEN=$(kubectl create token github-deployer -n my-app --duration=8760h)
SERVER=$(kubectl config view --minify -o jsonpath='{.clusters[0].cluster.server}')
CA=$(kubectl config view --minify --raw -o jsonpath='{.clusters[0].cluster.certificate-authority-data}')

cat > deployer.kubeconfig <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Config
clusters:
  - name: cluster
    cluster:
      server: $SERVER
      certificate-authority-data: $CA
users:
  - name: github-deployer
    user:
      token: $TOKEN
contexts:
  - name: deployer
    context:
      cluster: cluster
      user: github-deployer
      namespace: my-app
current-context: deployer
EOF

# Check it can do what the pipeline needs, and nothing more
kubectl --kubeconfig deployer.kubeconfig auth can-i patch deployments -n my-app   # yes
kubectl --kubeconfig deployer.kubeconfig auth can-i delete pods -n my-app         # no
```

In your repository, go to **Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions**, save the contents of `deployer.kubeconfig` as a secret named `KUBECONFIG`, and then delete the local file.

> **Note:** Some clusters cap how long a token can live. If yours does, `kubectl create token` gives you a shorter one, so note when it expires.

> **Tip:** On EKS, GKE or AKS you can skip long-lived tokens completely and use OpenID Connect (OIDC) so GitHub Actions gets short-lived cloud credentials. It's more setup, but it's the better long-term option.

## Step 3: Let the cluster pull from GHCR

If your package on GHCR is private, the cluster needs credentials to pull it. Create a GitHub personal access token with the `read:packages` scope and store it as an image pull secret:

```bash
kubectl create secret docker-registry ghcr-pull \
  --docker-server=ghcr.io \
  --docker-username=<github-username> \
  --docker-password=<token-with-read-packages> \
  -n my-app
```

Then reference it in the Deployment's pod spec:

```yaml
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      imagePullSecrets:
        - name: ghcr-pull
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: ghcr.io/<owner>/<app>:initial
```

## Step 4: The workflow

Save this as `.github/workflows/deploy.yml`:

```yaml
name: Build and deploy

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

env:
  IMAGE: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test

  build:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write   # lets GITHUB_TOKEN push to ghcr.io
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3
      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: |
            ${{ env.IMAGE }}:${{ github.sha }}
            ${{ env.IMAGE }}:latest
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production   # add required reviewers here for a manual approval step
    steps:
      - uses: azure/setup-kubectl@v4
      - name: Write kubeconfig
        run: |
          mkdir -p ~/.kube
          echo "${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG }}" > ~/.kube/config
          chmod 600 ~/.kube/config
      - name: Roll out the new image
        run: |
          kubectl set image deployment/my-app app=${{ env.IMAGE }}:${{ github.sha }} -n my-app
          kubectl rollout status deployment/my-app -n my-app --timeout=5m
```

What each part does:

- **`needs:`** chains the jobs, so a failing test stops the build, and a failing build stops the deploy.
- **`permissions: packages: write`** lets the built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN` push to GHCR. No extra registry secret is needed.
- **`cache-from` / `cache-to: type=gha`** stores Docker layers in the GitHub Actions cache, which cuts build time a lot.
- **`kubectl set image`** changes only the image, and Kubernetes does a rolling update: new pods start before old ones stop.
- **`kubectl rollout status`** waits until the new pods are ready. If they never become ready, the job fails and you see it straight away in GitHub.

> **Note:** GHCR image names must be lowercase. If your GitHub username or repository has capital letters, set `IMAGE` to a lowercase name yourself.

## Step 5: Make rollouts safe

A rolling update is only safe if Kubernetes can tell when a new pod is actually ready. Add a readiness probe and a rollout strategy to the Deployment:

```yaml
spec:
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 0   # never go below the current number of pods
      maxSurge: 1         # start one new pod at a time
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: app
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 3000
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 5
```

With `maxUnavailable: 0`, old pods keep serving traffic until each new pod passes its readiness probe. A broken release gets stuck at the first new pod instead of taking the whole app down, and `rollout status` fails the job.

## Step 6: Rolling back

Because every image is tagged with its commit SHA, you have two easy ways back:

```bash
# Go back to the previous ReplicaSet
kubectl rollout undo deployment/my-app -n my-app

# See the history and pick a specific revision
kubectl rollout history deployment/my-app -n my-app
kubectl rollout undo deployment/my-app -n my-app --to-revision=3
```

Or simply revert the bad commit in Git. The pipeline runs again and deploys the fixed version, so Git stays the record of what's running.

## Common problems

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `denied: permission_denied` when pushing | The job can't write packages | Add `permissions: packages: write` to the build job |
| Pods stuck in `ImagePullBackOff` | The cluster can't pull from GHCR | Check the `ghcr-pull` secret and `imagePullSecrets` |
| `invalid reference format` | Uppercase letters in the image name | Use a lowercase image name |
| `Forbidden` from `kubectl` | The ServiceAccount is missing a permission | Check the Role's `resources` and `verbs` |
| `rollout status` times out | New pods never become ready | `kubectl describe pod` and `kubectl logs` on the new pod |

## Wrapping up

With this setup, merging to `main` is the deployment. Tests guard the build, SHA tags make every release traceable, readiness probes stop broken releases before they reach users, and rolling back is a single command. From here, natural next steps are a staging environment that deploys first, and moving the Kubernetes manifests into Helm or Kustomize as the app grows.

attributes.title: How to Fix CrashLoopBackOff in Kubernetes
attributes.summary: A step-by-step guide to finding why a pod keeps crashing: reading pod events, previous logs and exit codes, and fixing out-of-memory kills, probe failures and bad config.
attributes.content:
`CrashLoopBackOff` is one of the most common errors in Kubernetes, and the name sounds scarier than it is. It does not tell you *what* is wrong. It only tells you that a container keeps crashing and Kubernetes is waiting longer and longer before restarting it. This guide is the step-by-step process I follow to find the real cause and fix it.

## What CrashLoopBackOff actually means

1. The container starts.
2. It exits or gets killed.
3. Kubernetes restarts it (because the pod's `restartPolicy` is `Always` or `OnFailure`).
4. It crashes again, and Kubernetes **backs off**: it waits 10s, then 20s, 40s and so on, up to 5 minutes, before the next try.

While it is waiting, the pod shows `CrashLoopBackOff`. If a container then runs fine for 10 minutes, the back-off timer resets.

```text
NAME                   READY   STATUS             RESTARTS      AGE
api-7f9c6d8b5-x2k4p    0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   5 (40s ago)   4m
```

> **Key idea:** CrashLoopBackOff is a *symptom*. The cause is always inside the container's last run, so the goal is to find out why that run ended.

## Step 1: Find the crashing pod

```bash
# Pods with restarts and their status
kubectl get pods -n <namespace>

# Across every namespace
kubectl get pods -A | grep -i crashloop
```

The `RESTARTS` column tells you how long this has been going on.

## Step 2: Describe the pod

```bash
kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n <namespace>
```

Look at two places in the output.

**The container's `Last State`**, which tells you how the previous run ended:

```text
    State:          Waiting
      Reason:       CrashLoopBackOff
    Last State:     Terminated
      Reason:       OOMKilled
      Exit Code:    137
```

**The `Events` at the bottom**, which show probe failures, image problems and restarts:

```text
Events:
  Warning  Unhealthy  Liveness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 500
  Warning  BackOff    Back-off restarting failed container api
```

## Step 3: Read the logs of the crashed run

The current container may have only just started, so its logs are often empty. Ask for the **previous** container instead:

```bash
# Logs from the run that crashed
kubectl logs <pod-name> -n <namespace> --previous

# Pick the container in a multi-container pod
kubectl logs <pod-name> -n <namespace> -c <container> --previous
```

Nine times out of ten, the answer is in the last few lines: a stack trace, a "connection refused", or a missing setting.

## Step 4: Decode the exit code

| Exit code | Meaning | Usual cause |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `0` | Exited normally | The process finished. Nothing kept it running (e.g. a script, or a wrong command) |
| `1` | Application error | The app crashed. Check the logs |
| `126` | Command not executable | Wrong file permissions on the entrypoint |
| `127` | Command not found | Typo in `command`/`args`, or the binary is missing from the image |
| `137` | Killed (SIGKILL) | Usually **OOMKilled**: it went over its memory limit |
| `139` | Segmentation fault | The program crashed in native code |
| `143` | Terminated (SIGTERM) | Stopped from outside, often by a failing liveness probe |

## Step 5: Fix the most common causes

### 1. The application itself is failing

The logs show an exception or "failed to start". Common reasons:

- A missing or wrong environment variable, such as a database URL.
- A dependency, like a database or another service, is not reachable yet.
- A bug in the new release.

Check what the container really gets:

```bash
kubectl exec <pod-name> -n <namespace> -- env    # works only while it is running
kubectl get deploy <name> -n <namespace> -o yaml | grep -A20 env:
```

If a bad release caused it, roll back while you investigate:

```bash
kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name> -n <namespace>
```

### 2. Out of memory (OOMKilled, exit code 137)

The container used more memory than its limit, so the kernel killed it. Check real usage, then raise the limit or fix the leak:

```bash
kubectl top pod <pod-name> -n <namespace>
```

```yaml
resources:
  requests:
    memory: "256Mi"
    cpu: "100m"
  limits:
    memory: "512Mi"
```

### 3. The liveness probe kills a healthy app

If the app needs 60 seconds to start but the liveness probe starts checking after 10, Kubernetes kills it before it is ready, every time. The events show `Liveness probe failed`.

Use a **startup probe**, so liveness checks only begin once the app is up:

```yaml
startupProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz
    port: 8080
  failureThreshold: 30     # 30 x 5s = up to 150s to start
  periodSeconds: 5
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz
    port: 8080
  periodSeconds: 10
```

Also check that the probe's `path` and `port` actually exist in your app.

### 4. Wrong command or arguments (exit code 0, 126 or 127)

A `command` in the manifest replaces the image's entrypoint. A typo, or a command that runs and exits straight away, causes a loop. Compare the manifest with what the image expects:

```bash
kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].command} {.spec.containers[0].args}'
```

### 5. Missing permissions or files

Errors like `permission denied` or `read-only file system` usually come from the `securityContext` (for example `runAsNonRoot` or `readOnlyRootFilesystem`) or from a volume mounted over a path the app needs to write to.

> **Not the same error:** a missing ConfigMap or Secret usually shows as `CreateContainerConfigError`, and a bad image shows as `ImagePullBackOff`. Those happen *before* the container runs, so they are fixed differently.

## Step 6: Debug inside the container

When the container dies too fast to `exec` into, use `kubectl debug`.

```bash
# Attach a temporary debug container to the running pod
kubectl debug -it <pod-name> -n <namespace> --image=busybox:1.36 --target=<container>

# Or make a copy of the pod whose container just runs a shell
kubectl debug <pod-name> -n <namespace> -it --copy-to=<pod-name>-debug --container=<container> -- sh
```

The copy keeps the same image, environment and volumes, so you can run the app by hand and watch it fail. Delete the copy when you are done:

```bash
kubectl delete pod <pod-name>-debug -n <namespace>
```

## Quick checklist

1. `kubectl get pods` to find the pod and its restart count.
2. `kubectl describe pod` and read **Last State**, **Exit Code** and **Events**.
3. `kubectl logs --previous` to see why the last run ended.
4. Match the exit code: `1` for an app error, `137` for out of memory, `143` for a failing probe.
5. Fix the cause: config, memory limits, probes, command or permissions.
6. Still stuck? Use `kubectl debug` and run the app by hand.

> **Using K9s?** Select the pod and press `d` to describe it and `p` for the previous logs. See my [K9s Cheat Sheet](/blog/k9s-cheat-sheet).

seo.metaDescription: A step-by-step guide to debugging CrashLoopBackOff pods in Kubernetes.

attributes.title: K9s Cheat Sheet
attributes.summary: Keyboard shortcuts and commands for K9s, the terminal UI for Kubernetes: navigation, logs, shells, port-forwards, scaling and filtering.
attributes.content:
[K9s](https://k9scli.io/) is a terminal UI for Kubernetes. Instead of typing long `kubectl` commands, you move around your cluster with the keyboard: list pods, read logs, open a shell, scale a deployment, all from one screen. This is my quick reference for the keys I use every day.

> **Tip:** You never need to memorise everything. Press `?` in any view to see every key available there, and the top of the screen always shows the most useful shortcuts.

## Install and launch

```bash
# Install (pick one)
brew install derailed/k9s/k9s        # macOS / Linux with Homebrew
winget install k9s                    # Windows
go install github.com/derailed/k9s@latest

# Start with your current kube context
k9s

# Start in a specific namespace, or all namespaces
k9s -n <namespace>
k9s -A

# Start with a specific context
k9s --context <context-name>

# Open straight into a resource view
k9s -c deploy

# Read-only mode: no edits or deletes (great for production)
k9s --readonly

# Show where K9s keeps its config, logs and skins
k9s info
```

## Moving around

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `?` | Help: every key for the current view |
| `:` | Command mode: jump to a resource, e.g. `:pod` |
| `/` | Filter the current list |
| `Esc` | Go back, or clear a filter |
| `Enter` | Drill down (e.g. deployment → pods → containers) |
| `j` / `k` or arrows | Move down / up |
| `Ctrl-a` | List every resource and alias |
| `:q` or `Ctrl-c` | Quit |

## Jump to a resource

Type these in command mode (`:`). Short names work just like in `kubectl`.

```text
:pod     or :po      Pods
:deploy  or :dp      Deployments
:svc                 Services
:ing                 Ingresses
:no                  Nodes
:ns                  Namespaces
:cm                  ConfigMaps
:sec                 Secrets
:pvc                 Persistent volume claims
:job / :cj           Jobs / CronJobs
:ds / :sts           DaemonSets / StatefulSets
:ev                  Events
:ctx                 Contexts (switch cluster)
:helm                Helm releases
:crd                 Custom resource definitions
:pu                  Pulses: live cluster overview
:xray deploy         Tree view of deployments and what they own
```

You can add a namespace after the resource, for example `:pod kube-system`.

## Namespaces and contexts

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `:ns` then `Enter` | Pick a namespace |
| `0` | Show all namespaces (in a resource view) |
| `1`–`9` | Switch to a recently used namespace (listed at the top) |
| `:ctx` then `Enter` | Switch to another cluster/context |

## Working with any resource

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `d` | Describe |
| `y` | View YAML |
| `e` | Edit in your `$EDITOR` |
| `Ctrl-d` | Delete (asks to confirm) |
| `Space` | Mark an item, to act on several at once |
| `Ctrl-w` | Toggle wide columns |
| `Ctrl-z` | Show only resources with errors |
| `Ctrl-s` | Save the current list to a file |

**Sorting** (works in most list views):

| Key | Sort by |
| --- | --- |
| `Shift-n` | Name |
| `Shift-a` | Age |
| `Shift-s` | Status |
| `Shift-c` | CPU |
| `Shift-m` | Memory |

## Pods

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `l` | Logs |
| `p` | Logs of the previous (crashed) container |
| `s` | Open a shell inside the container |
| `a` | Attach to the container |
| `Shift-f` | Port-forward to the pod |
| `o` | Jump to the node the pod runs on |
| `Ctrl-k` | Kill the pod immediately (no confirmation) |
| `Enter` | List the pod's containers |

> **Careful:** `Ctrl-k` deletes the pod without asking. Use `k9s --readonly` when you only want to look around a production cluster.

## Deployments, StatefulSets and DaemonSets

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `s` | Scale replicas |
| `r` | Rollout restart |
| `i` | Set a new container image |
| `l` | Logs from all its pods |
| `Enter` | See its pods |

## Logs view

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `/` | Filter log lines |
| `s` | Toggle auto-scroll |
| `w` | Toggle line wrap |
| `t` | Toggle timestamps |
| `f` | Toggle full screen |
| `0`–`6` | Change the time range (options are shown at the top) |
| `Ctrl-s` | Save the logs to a file |
| `Esc` | Back to the list |

## Filtering tricks

```text
/nginx            Rows containing "nginx"
/!nginx           Rows NOT containing "nginx"
/-l app=nginx     Filter by label
/-f ngnx          Fuzzy search
```

Filters stay active while you work. Press `Esc` to clear them.

## Port-forwards

```text
Shift-f    in a pod or service view: create a port-forward
:pf        list active port-forwards
Ctrl-d     in the :pf view: stop a port-forward
```

## Customising K9s

Run `k9s info` to find the config folder. Inside it you can add:

- **`config.yaml`**: general settings, such as refresh rate and read-only mode.
- **`aliases.yaml`**: your own shortcuts, e.g. map `:dp` to deployments.
- **`hotkeys.yaml`**: one-key jumps, e.g. `Shift-0` to open pods.
- **`plugins.yaml`**: run your own commands on the selected resource.
- **`skins/`**: colour themes.

A simple alias file looks like this:

```yaml
aliases:
  dp: apps/v1/deployments
  sec: v1/secrets
  jo: batch/v1/jobs
```

## Daily workflow

1. `k9s -n my-app` to open the app's namespace.
2. `:pod` and `/api` to find the pod.
3. `l` for logs, `p` if it just crashed.
4. `s` to shell in and check config or connectivity.
5. `:dp`, select the deployment, `r` to restart once it is fixed.

seo.metaDescription: Keyboard shortcuts and commands for K9s, the terminal UI for Kubernetes.

attributes.title: Kubernetes Command Cheat Sheet
attributes.summary: A quick reference of the kubectl commands I use most: contexts, pods, deployments, rollouts, logs, debugging, networking and node maintenance.
attributes.content:
A quick reference for the `kubectl` commands I use most when working with Kubernetes clusters. Keep it open in a tab and copy what you need.

> **Tip:** Most commands accept `-n <namespace>` to target a namespace, or `-A` to run across all namespaces.

## Setup and shortcuts

```bash
# Short alias: type "k" instead of "kubectl"
alias k=kubectl

# Enable tab completion (bash)
source <(kubectl completion bash)

# Check client and server versions
kubectl version
```

## Contexts and namespaces

```bash
# List all contexts in your kubeconfig
kubectl config get-contexts

# Show the current context
kubectl config current-context

# Switch to another cluster/context
kubectl config use-context <context-name>

# Set the default namespace for the current context
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=<namespace>

# List namespaces
kubectl get namespaces

# Create a namespace
kubectl create namespace <namespace>
```

## Cluster information

```bash
# Control plane and core service addresses
kubectl cluster-info

# List nodes with IPs, OS and runtime
kubectl get nodes -o wide

# Detailed info about a node (capacity, conditions, pods)
kubectl describe node <node-name>

# Resource types the cluster supports
kubectl api-resources
```

## Viewing resources

```bash
# Pods in the current namespace
kubectl get pods

# Pods in all namespaces, with node and IP
kubectl get pods -A -o wide

# Watch pods change live
kubectl get pods -w

# Several resource types at once
kubectl get deploy,svc,ingress

# Filter by label
kubectl get pods -l app=<app-name>

# Full details and recent events for a pod
kubectl describe pod <pod-name>

# Full YAML of a live object
kubectl get deployment <name> -o yaml

# Sort pods by restart count
kubectl get pods --sort-by='.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount'
```

## Creating and applying

```bash
# Create or update from a file (declarative, preferred)
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml

# Apply every manifest in a folder
kubectl apply -f ./k8s/

# Preview what apply would change
kubectl diff -f deployment.yaml

# Create a deployment quickly
kubectl create deployment <name> --image=nginx:1.27 --replicas=2

# Generate YAML without creating anything
kubectl create deployment <name> --image=nginx:1.27 --dry-run=client -o yaml > deployment.yaml

# Store config and secrets
kubectl create configmap <name> --from-literal=KEY=value
kubectl create secret generic <name> --from-literal=PASSWORD=changeme
```

## Deployments and rollouts

```bash
# Scale a deployment
kubectl scale deployment <name> --replicas=5

# Update the container image
kubectl set image deployment/<name> <container>=nginx:1.27.1

# Follow a rollout until it finishes
kubectl rollout status deployment/<name>

# Rollout history
kubectl rollout history deployment/<name>

# Roll back to the previous version
kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>

# Roll back to a specific revision
kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name> --to-revision=2

# Restart all pods (for example after a config change)
kubectl rollout restart deployment/<name>

# Autoscale on CPU usage
kubectl autoscale deployment <name> --min=2 --max=10 --cpu-percent=70
```

## Logs and debugging

```bash
# Pod logs
kubectl logs <pod-name>

# Follow logs live
kubectl logs -f <pod-name>

# A specific container in a multi-container pod
kubectl logs <pod-name> -c <container>

# Logs from the crashed previous container
kubectl logs <pod-name> --previous

# Last hour, last 100 lines
kubectl logs <pod-name> --since=1h --tail=100

# Logs from every pod of a deployment
kubectl logs deployment/<name> --all-containers

# Open a shell inside a pod
kubectl exec -it <pod-name> -- sh

# Run a single command in a pod
kubectl exec <pod-name> -- env

# Recent cluster events, newest last
kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp

# Start a throwaway debug pod
kubectl run debug --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 -- sh
```

## Networking

```bash
# Forward a local port to a pod
kubectl port-forward pod/<pod-name> 8080:80

# Forward a local port to a service
kubectl port-forward svc/<service-name> 8080:80

# Expose a deployment as a service
kubectl expose deployment <name> --port=80 --target-port=8080 --type=ClusterIP

# List services and endpoints
kubectl get svc,endpoints
```

## Resource usage

These need the metrics-server add-on installed in the cluster.

```bash
# CPU and memory per node
kubectl top nodes

# CPU and memory per pod, highest first
kubectl top pods -A --sort-by=memory
```

## Copying files

```bash
# Copy from a pod to your machine
kubectl cp <namespace>/<pod-name>:/path/in/pod ./local-file

# Copy from your machine to a pod
kubectl cp ./local-file <namespace>/<pod-name>:/path/in/pod
```

## Deleting resources

```bash
# Delete what a file created
kubectl delete -f deployment.yaml

# Delete a single pod (its deployment will create a new one)
kubectl delete pod <pod-name>

# Delete everything with a label
kubectl delete pods -l app=<app-name>

# Delete a namespace and everything in it
kubectl delete namespace <namespace>
```

> **Careful:** `kubectl delete namespace` removes every resource inside it. Double-check your context with `kubectl config current-context` before running destructive commands.

## Node maintenance

```bash
# Stop new pods from being scheduled on a node
kubectl cordon <node-name>

# Move pods off a node before maintenance
kubectl drain <node-name> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data

# Allow scheduling again
kubectl uncordon <node-name>
```

## Handy output formats

```bash
# Just the names
kubectl get pods -o name

# Custom columns
kubectl get pods -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,STATUS:.status.phase

# Pull one field with JSONPath
kubectl get pod <pod-name> -o jsonpath='{.status.podIP}'

# Explain any field of a resource
kubectl explain deployment.spec.strategy
```

seo.metaDescription: A quick reference of the most useful kubectl commands.
